newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq supports cereal prices to protect farmers.
newsitem.headline: Iraq supports cereal prices to protect farmers.

text.p: Iraq is paying above the market price for cereals to protect farmers from the impact of the oil-for-food deal with the United Nations, traders said on Tuesday.
They said the aim was to defend farmers' income and encourage them to continue cultivation of wheat, barley, rice and other commercial crops such as sunflowers and maize.
The government was offering to pay at or above local market rates in the face of supplies piling up under the agreement allowing Baghdad to export some oil in return for food and medicine.
For the first time since sanctions were clamped on Iraq in 1990 for invading Kuwait, farmers have the option to either ship their produce to state silos or sell direct to traders on the open market.
Previously, farmers said, they were obliged to ship their wheat, barley, rice and other crops to the state at pre-determined prices. Violators were threatened with prison and confiscation of crops.
About 900,000 tonnes of food have arrived in Iraq since it started exporting limited quantities of oil in December last year to meet urgent needs.
For a tonne of wheat the government pays up to 120,00 dinars, about $75 at the current exchange rate. For barley it offers up to 80,000 dinars.

The government newspaper al-Jumhoriya said the government was also ready to buy other crops like sunflowers, maize and rice. The state-purchasing price for maize is about 105,000 dinars a tonne, 250,000 for sunflower and up to 185,000 for rice, depending on quality.

The flow of food supplies under the oil deal has led to a drop in prices included in Iraq's ration card, namely, flour, sugar and rice. Flour slipped to about 300 dinars from 500 and rice to 350 from 600.

The first six months of the deal worth $2 billion ended in June. The U.N. Security Council has renewed the plan but is still awaiting Iraq's procurement and distribution plans to give it the go ahead to resume partial exports again.

Iraq planned to import more than two million tonnes of food supplies in the first six months but it has so far only received about half the amount due to delays in approving the contracts which Baghdad blames on the United States.

Statistics on crop production are among Iraq's closely guarded secrets. U.N. relief workers say a bumper harvest would only provide Iraq with about 2.5 million tonnes at a time when its needs exceed four million.
No forecast is available for this year's harvest. Last year the U.N. said Iraq's harvest was at least one million tonnes short of expectations but the government said it was more than satisfactory.
Prior to the U.N. embargo, Iraq earmarked up to $5 billion for purchases of wheat, rice and sugar with wheat and rice shipments coming mainly from the United States.
